blocks.text: In 1952 the American biologists Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase did experiments to confirm that DNA is the genetic material, using bacteriophages, viruses that attack bacteria.

Background: a bacteriophage has a core of DNA or RNA and a protein coat. A lytic phage binds to the surface of a bacterium and injects some material into the cell; this material is hereditary, because it directs the making of new phages inside the bacterium, which finally bursts (lyses) and releases them. The question was which material, nucleic acid or protein or both, the phage injects.

blocks.alt: Two rows. Setup 1: phages with an orange 35S-labelled protein coat infect a bacterium; after blending and spinning, the radioactivity is in the liquid with the empty phage coats. Setup 2: phages with blue 32P-labelled DNA infect a bacterium; after blending and spinning, the radioactivity is in the pellet of bacteria.
blocks.caption: The two setups of Hershey and Chase (original diagram after Figure 19.7).
blocks.long_description: In 1952 Hershey and Chase used a DNA-containing bacteriophage. They grew some phages with radioactive sulphur, 35S, which enters the amino acids of the protein coat, and others with radioactive phosphorus, 32P, which enters the phosphate groups of DNA. Each kind was allowed to infect bacteria; the cells and the medium were then separated by centrifugation and tested. With 35S the radioactivity stayed in the medium, not in the bacteria; with 32P it was in the bacterial cells. So the phage DNA entered the bacteria and directed the making of new phages, while the protein coat stayed outside.

items: They used a phage containing DNA, not RNA, and labelled its parts with different radioactive isotopes as tracers.
Some phages were grown with sulphur-35 (35S), which entered the amino acids of the protein coats; others with phosphorus-32 (32P), which entered the phosphate groups of the DNA.
Setup 1: phages with 35S-labelled protein infected bacteria. Setup 2: phages with 32P-labelled DNA infected bacteria.
After some time the infected cells and the medium were separated by centrifugation and tested for radioactivity.

blocks.text: So during infection the 32P-labelled DNA entered the bacterial cells and directed the making of new phages, while the 35S-labelled protein coat stayed outside. Hershey and Chase concluded that the phage DNA, not the protein, directs the production of new phages.

blocks.prompt: Why were sulphur and phosphorus chosen as the two labels?
blocks.explanation: Proteins contain sulphur (in some amino acids) but DNA does not; DNA contains phosphorus (in its phosphate groups) but protein has little. So each isotope marks only one of the two.

items: 35S labels phage protein; 32P labels phage DNA.
32P entered the bacteria; 35S stayed in the medium.
DNA, not protein, directs new phages.
